newsitem.title: UK: Britain launches review of North Sea oil tax.
newsitem.headline: Britain launches review of North Sea oil tax.

text.p: Britain has launched a review of North Sea petroleum taxation probably in time for the government's next budget in the spring.
A study has been ordered by the Treasury in tandem with the Inland Revenue and the Department of Trade and Industry, a government spokeswoman said on Monday.
"The review is to see whether we're taxing an appropriate share of profits with a view to maintaining the high level of interest in the future development of reserves," the spokeswoman said.
She could not immediately confirm the time frame for the review.

It will prompt oil industry concerns that the new Labour government is preparing to clamp down on what is widely recognised as the world's most lenient fiscal regime among major oil producing countries.
Geneva-based Petroconsultants calculates that only Ireland, a minor oil province, offers oil companies a more favourable tax regime.

Oil companies in British waters are liable only to 31 percent corporation tax on fields developed since 1993 which was when the former Conservative government abolished Petroleum Revenue Tax (PRT) for new developments.
PRT for existing fields was reduced at that time from 75 percent to 50 percent. Royalty at 12.5 percent applies to oilfields given development approval before April 1982.
Combined British oil and gas tax receipts in the fiscal 1996/1997 jumped to 3.6 billion pounds from 2.35 billion the year before.
But the tax take still lags the record 12.171 billion pounds collected in 1984/85 when total company income was at similar levels to that of last year.
